note: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok recalled studying with Rabbi Yohanan the Horani, a disciple of Beit Shammai, who in years of drought ate dry bread with salt. Rabbi Elazar's father sent him olives, but Rabbi Yohanan saw they were moist with their own juice, which could make them susceptible to ritual impurity, and politely said: I do not eat olives. When Rabbi Elazar told his father, the father sent word that the barrel had been perforated and then clogged by sediment, so the olives had not become susceptible. The text does not say what Rabbi Yohanan did next.
why: The Gemara is asking whether Beit Shammai actually practised by their own rulings where they disagreed with Beit Hillel; the teaching adds that Rabbi Yohanan the Horani always followed Beit Hillel, which is praise only if Beit Shammai's followers usually followed their own view.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok
people.about: The teller, who studied with Rabbi Yohanan the Horani and brought him olives from his father.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan the Horani
people.about: A disciple of Beit Shammai who lived on bread and salt in years of drought.

terms.meaning: Food can become ritually impure only after it has been made wet by certain liquids, such as olive oil, with the owner's consent.
A barrel with a hole bored in it to let the olive juice drain out, showing the owner did not want the juice on the olives.
Two early schools of Sages that often disagreed; the law usually follows Beit Hillel.

note: When Rav came to the town of Dardeshir, he made a public announcement: Which woman will be my wife for the day? Rav Nahman did the same when he came to Shakhnetziv. Both Sages, away from home, publicly sought a wife for the length of their stay.
why: Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov taught that a man should not marry wives in different countries, lest his children meet and unknowingly marry each other; the Gemara asks how these Sages could do so, and answers that a Sage's children are always known as his.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who sought a wife for the day when visiting Dardeshir.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who did the same when visiting Shakhnetziv.

note: Rabbi Elazar taught a ruling of Rabbi Yohanan in the study hall without naming him, and Rabbi Yohanan was angry. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi tried to calm him by recalling how Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei once argued in a Tiberias synagogue until a Torah scroll tore, and Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma predicted the synagogue would become a place of idol worship, as it did. That made Rabbi Yohanan angrier: were they now making him and his student colleagues? Then Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi pointed out that Joshua taught without saying Moses told me, yet everyone knew it was Moses' Torah; so too everyone knew Rabbi Elazar's teaching came from Rabbi Yohanan. Rabbi Yohanan was appeased and asked the other two why they could not appease him that way.
why: The Gemara has just explained a ruling about levirate marriage that Rabbi Elazar taught without naming Rabbi Yohanan; afterwards it explains his anger: when a teaching is repeated in a scholar's name, his lips move in the grave.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Rabbi Elazar's teacher, angered that his ruling was taught without his name.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: Rabbi Yohanan's beloved disciple, who taught the ruling without naming him.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: With Rabbi Asi, tried and failed to calm Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: With Rabbi Ami, tried and failed to calm Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi
people.about: The Sage who succeeded in appeasing Rabbi Yohanan.

terms.meaning: Things set aside from use on Shabbat, which may not be moved; the question was whether a door bolt counted as a usable vessel or as raw material.
The house of study where the Sages taught and debated.

note: In the town of Neresh, a woman had been betrothed as a minor and then came of age. Her husband seated her in the bridal chair under the marriage canopy, but before they had been together, another man came, seized her from him, and married her. Rav's students Rav Bruna and Rav Hananel were there, and they did not require her to receive a bill of divorce from the second man.
why: The Gemara is checking Rav's view that a marriage to a girl betrothed as a minor is complete only after intercourse once she is an adult; this case seems to contradict it, and Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi then explain it away.

people.name: Rav Bruna
people.about: A student of Rav, present at the incident.

people.name: Rav Hananel
people.about: A student of Rav, present at the incident.

terms.meaning: A young girl could be married off by her family before adulthood; the Sages debate whether that marriage is fully binding once she grows up.
The get, the document needed to end a valid marriage; not requiring one means the second marriage never took effect.

note: Rav Yitzhak bar Bisna lost the keys to the study hall in the public domain, and on Shabbat no one could carry them back. He asked Rabbi Pedat what to do. Rabbi Pedat told him to take boys and girls to walk where the keys were lost: if they found the keys, they would bring them of their own accord, without anyone telling them to.
why: From Rabbi Pedat's advice the Gemara infers that a court need not stop a child from breaking a prohibition, and then tests that idea against other teachings about children and gentiles on Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Bisna
people.about: The man who lost the keys to the study hall.

people.name: Rabbi Pedat
people.about: The Sage who advised him to let children find the keys.

terms.meaning: Open public space such as a street; on Shabbat it is forbidden to carry objects there.
A child not yet obligated in the commandments; the question is whether adults must stop children who break them.
